name: Edison Grid
description:
Edison Grid is the neighborhood that polices itself and doesn't apologize for it. The far northwest corner of GLMZ, Edison Park was always Chicago's most suburban enclave — tidy bungalows, neat lawns, families where both parents worked for the city. Police officers, firefighters, paramedics, public works employees. When the corporations privatized everything, Edison Park's residents found themselves in a unique position: they were the people who'd kept the old city running, and the new city needed their skills even if it didn't want their independence. Axiom Security Solutions absorbed the police force. Corporate emergency services absorbed the fire department. The old public servants became corporate contractors with better salaries and fewer rights. But they kept living in Edison Park, kept raising their families on the same blocks, and kept the one thing the corps couldn't privatize: the institutional knowledge of how a city actually works, passed down through families like a genetic trait.

The Grid earned its name from the power infrastructure. When GLMZ's energy grid was being built, Edison Park's residents — many of them electrical workers and engineers by trade — negotiated a deal that no other neighborhood managed: a dedicated power substation feeding the district directly, bypassing the corporate metering system. It was supposed to be temporary. That was thirty years ago. The Grid still has the most reliable electricity in Meridian's outlying districts, and the substation has been quietly expanded, modified, and hardened by residents who understand power systems the way other people understand cooking. The electricity is technically corporate property. The Grid's position is that they built the system, they maintain the system, and anyone who wants to renegotiate can discuss it with the electricians' union, which is also the neighborhood militia.

The culture of Edison Grid is cop culture — for better and worse. The streets are orderly. Crime is low. Community standards are enforced by social pressure and, when necessary, by retired Axiom Security contractors who still have their training and most of their augments. There's a code: you look out for your neighbors, you maintain your property, you don't bring trouble home. It's effective and stifling in equal measure. The Grid's children grow up safe and grow up to leave, because safety and predictability are not the same as freedom. The ones who stay become cops or electricians or both, and the cycle continues.

The Grid's relationship with Axiom Security is the district's defining tension. Many residents work for the corporation. Many residents distrust the corporation. These are often the same people. An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer follows corporate orders during shift and comes home to a neighborhood that views corporate authority with the skeptical eye of people who remember when authority was public and accountable. This cognitive dissonance produces a population that is simultaneously Axiom's most competent workforce and its most quietly resistant. The Grid doesn't rebel. It doesn't protest. It maintains its power substation, trains its children in skills the corporation needs, and waits — with the patience of people who understand infrastructure — for the system to need them more than they need it.

sights: Neat residential blocks — bungalows maintained to standards that would have been normal in the old city and are remarkable now
The power substation at the district's center, expanded and reinforced over decades, humming with dedicated electricity
Retired security contractors walking patrol routes out of habit, augmented eyes scanning without urgency
Family gardens in every yard — practical vegetables, not decorative landscaping
The Blue Line terminal at the district's edge — the last stop, literally and figuratively, before the suburban wastelands begin
Memorial plaques on homes — names of officers and firefighters who died in service, maintained by families who remember
sounds: The hum of the power substation — louder than you'd expect, a low throb that residents stop hearing after a week
Children playing in actual yards — one of the few districts where outdoor play space exists
Scanner chatter from homes where off-duty security personnel keep a radio on — old habit, professional compulsion
The Blue Line train arriving and departing — a schedule so reliable it functions as a neighborhood clock
Quiet — but a different quiet than the Palisade. This is the quiet of a place where trouble knows better than to make noise.
smells: Grilled food from backyard cookouts — the Grid maintains a cookout culture that is part social tradition and part defiant normalcy
Ozone from the power substation, strongest in humid weather
Cut grass — real grass, maintained by hand, a point of pride
Coffee from kitchens in the morning — the Grid wakes up early because shift work starts early
atmosphere.feel: Controlled. Edison Grid feels like a place where everything works because someone made it work and continues to make it work through daily effort and communal will. It's reassuring and claustrophobic — the safety is real, the order is real, and the social pressure to conform is equally real. The Grid is what a neighborhood looks like when the people who run the city's systems build a place for themselves. It's functional. It's dependable. It's not a place that welcomes questions about whether there might be a better way.

demographics: Approximately 10,000 residents, predominantly Tier 2 and Tier 3. Multigenerational families with backgrounds in public safety, infrastructure maintenance, and emergency services. Racially and ethnically mixed but culturally uniform — the shared identity is occupational, not ethnic. The most stable population in Meridian's northwest.
economy: Skilled labor export — Edison Grid's residents work throughout Meridian's infrastructure and security sectors. The power substation generates surplus electricity that's traded to neighboring districts. Small-scale commercial services support the residential population. The economy is wages, not entrepreneurship.
power_structure: The Grid Council — elected from resident families, heavily weighted toward senior infrastructure and security workers. The electricians' union holds veto power over energy-related decisions. Axiom has no direct governance role but exercises influence through the employment relationship with most working-age residents.
dangers: Social conformity enforcement — deviance from community standards is punished by isolation and ostracism
The Axiom loyalty question — residents who are seen as too corporate or too resistant to corporate authority face suspicion from both sides
Power substation dependency — the Grid's independence is built on infrastructure that could be targeted
Insularity — outsiders are tolerated but not trusted, and the Grid's closed culture limits information exchange
The militia's competence — Edison Grid's residents are trained, equipped, and organized enough to be dangerous if the wrong situation triggers a response
opportunities: Reliable power — the Grid's electricity supply is a strategic resource in a city of rolling blackouts
Skilled labor connections — the Grid's workers have access to every level of Meridian's infrastructure
Institutional knowledge — these families know how the city works in ways that blueprints don't capture
Security expertise — retired Axiom personnel with training and augments, available for contract work if the cause is right
The Blue Line terminal — the last transit connection to the northwestern suburbs, a smuggling route that the Grid quietly tolerates
story_hooks: An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer discovers that the corporation is planning to bypass the neighborhood's power substation — routing the Grid into the metered system. The Grid Council prepares for a confrontation that could turn the district's quiet resistance into open conflict.

Kyle needs information that only an active Axiom Security officer can access. The officer is Edison Grid — loyal to the community first, the corporation second. The price of the information is a favor that puts Kyle on the wrong side of people he'd rather not cross.

A Grid family's child returns from a stint in the Shelf with augments, ideas, and associations that violate everything the community stands for. The family is torn between protecting their own and maintaining the social contract that keeps the Grid functioning.
frequented_by: Multigenerational families with roots in public safety and infrastructure work
Off-duty Axiom Security personnel living among the community they serve and question
Electricians and infrastructure workers maintaining the power substation and trading surplus energy
Blue Line commuters — the terminal is a transit point for anyone moving between Meridian and the northwest
The occasional outsider buying surplus power or hiring skilled labor, tolerated but watched
